opening.headline: Read the risk management system disclosed by the provider and explain the structure in which distribution conditions vary depending on ability level.
body: If our team only uses the model's document summary function, the provider's risk management framework may seem like someone else's story. However, providers promise not to deploy models that exceed a certain level of capability until safeguards are in place, and this promise translates into additional controls and the scope of features available to us.

In this class, you will learn how to read what risks OpenAI's Preparedness Framework handles, how the risk areas are divided, and what changes when the capability thresholds, High and Critical, are reached. At the end, we follow the distribution decision flow of the model that has exceeded the threshold step by step.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain risk areas and response measures in the Preparedness Framework
Can distinguish between actions when a capability threshold is reached

screens.title: What does the provider’s risk management system have to do with us?
screens.lead: Read the situation below from the perspective of a team that only uses document summarization. It's a great read to think about how a provider's safety commitment can impact this team.

visual.alt: A flowchart of the provider's risk management commitments leading to the scope of available features and additional controls.
labels: Our team plans to use it

paragraphs: One team is only using the document summarization function of an AI model. To this team, the risk management framework created by the model provider feels like a document that should concern frontline labs and not their own.

However, this document is a public promise that the provider will keep. It states that models with capabilities exceeding a certain level will not be distributed until safety measures are in place to sufficiently reduce the risk. These promises determine what features will be provided, when, and under what terms.
So those planning to use it should also be able to read this document. This class covers how to read what OpenAI's Preparedness Framework promises.

screens.outro: First, let me recall my experience with these documents.

screens.title: Did you know there is a risk assessment at model launch?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Did you know there is a risk assessment at model launch?
items.answer: When providers roll out new models, they assess capabilities and risks and make the results public. OpenAI explains that it has been releasing Preparedness-related results together with each release of its front-line model. Knowing that this assessment exists is a starting point.

items.prompt: Have you ever opened your model card or system card?
items.answer: These documents describe how the model has been evaluated and what its limitations are. If you've never opened it, you still don't know what this framework will look like. The framework for reading in this class becomes the foundation for understanding such documents.

items.prompt: Have you factored into your plan that your provider may withhold or limit distribution?
items.answer: The framework stipulates that deployment may be withheld or restricted if safeguards are not sufficient. If your usage plans depend on a particular feature, you should also factor in the possibility that that feature may be limited. It is safer to think about alternatives in advance.

screens.outro: Now that you're ready to read the documentation, let's first look at the structure of the framework.

screens.title: Structure of framework documents
screens.lead: Select a number marker to see a detailed description of what each part of the document covers. Follow how the document defines risks and explains them in what order.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the table of contents of the framework document arranged into four large columns and appendices with numbered markers.
labels: Appendix: Decision methods, examples of safeguards

markers.label: where to focus
markers.title: Limit the risk to extreme damage
markers.body: The framework is OpenAI's approach to tracking and preparing for frontline capabilities that can create new risks. Severe harm here means thousands of deaths or serious injuries, or hundreds of billions of dollars in economic damage. Lower level hazards are covered by other safety systems, so this document does not cover all hazards.

markers.label: ability measurement
markers.title: Measure ability through evaluation
markers.body: Decide how to evaluate what capabilities your model has. We use a combination of automated assessments that are easy to run repeatedly and in-depth assessments that experts dig deep into. The evaluation results determine whether the competency threshold has been reached.

markers.label: safety device
markers.title: Safety device against extreme damage
markers.body: It deals with the criteria for selecting safety devices, safety device sufficiency, which determines whether the safety device sufficiently reduces the risk, and marginal risk. Sufficiency is the step to check whether the safety device sufficiently reduces the risk, and marginal risk is a perspective that looks at how much additional risk is created compared to the risk that already exists elsewhere.

markers.label: Building trust
markers.title: Internal governance and external participation
markers.body: It addresses internal governance, transparency, and external participation. A Safety Advisory Group (SAG) made up of cross-functional leaders recommends the level and type of safeguards needed, which management approves or rejects, and the board's Safety and Security Committee oversees these decisions.

markers.label: appendix
markers.title: Examples of safety devices
markers.body: The appendix contains examples of safety devices. Safeguards against malicious users, safeguards against misaligned models, and security controls are outlined. This example shows specifically what kind of safeguards are expected.

screens.outro: Now that we know the structure, let’s look at the table to see which risk areas the framework addresses.

screens.title: Risk Areas: Tracking Category and Study Category
screens.lead: The table below shows how the framework divides the risk areas. See how the tracking and research categories differ and what beneficial uses each area has.

data.caption: Risk areas in the Preparedness Framework
rows: The ability to lower the barriers to entry to make and use biological and chemical weapons while enabling discoveries and treatments.
Ability to help protect vulnerable systems while also creating new risks of large-scale cyberattacks and vulnerability exploitation
The ability to unlock useful capabilities more quickly while also creating new challenges for human control of AI systems.
Long-term autonomy, sandbagging, autonomous replication and adaptation, neutralization of safety devices, nuclear and radioactivity
Areas that do not yet meet the criteria for the tracking category but could result in extreme damage and for which threat models and assessments are being developed.
data.notes: All three tracking categories are dual-use, with both beneficial uses and risks. Five criteria determine which abilities to track: Is it plausible, measurable, serious, novel, immediate, or irreversible? Persuasion risks are addressed outside of this framework through methods such as Model Specs and restrictions on their use for political campaigns and lobbying, and detection of influence operations. The research category means that the assessments are not as mature as the current tracking category, so this area should not be read as lacking safeguards needs, but rather as an area where providers will evolve their threat models and assessments in the future.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the areas, let's get moving and see what changes once we reach the ability threshold.

screens.title: Commentary: Ability threshold High and Critical
screens.lead: Move the sliders to see how the required safeguards change as your model's ability level increases. The instructor explains what each step means.

visual.alt: A horizontal bar diagram showing the ability levels divided into three categories and the safety measures required for each category at different times.
labels: Safety devices are required even during development

stops.body: The ability has not yet reached the High threshold. In this case too, the provider manages the risk with its usual safeguards framework, but the additional safeguards requirements required by the framework do not apply. However, the evaluation continues, and when new evidence emerges, it is re-determined whether the threshold has been reached.

High abilities can amplify existing paths that lead to extreme damage. Systems that reach this level must have safeguards in place before deployment to sufficiently reduce the associated risk of extreme harm. For example, in the biological and chemical domains, safeguards against misuse and security controls must meet high standards before external deployment.

Critical abilities are levels that can open up unprecedented new paths. At this level, safeguards are needed to sufficiently reduce risk before deployment as well as during development. Area-specific guidelines include measures to halt further development until safeguards and security controls that meet those standards are in place.

Whether any level of safeguarding is sufficient is reviewed by the Safety Advisory Group (SAG). SAG makes recommendations, which are approved or rejected by management and overseen by the board's Safety and Security Committee. This structure ensures that deployment decisions are not left to the discretion of one team.

screens.outro: Now let's follow the order in which distribution decisions for models that have passed the threshold are made.

screens.title: Explanation: A flow whose distribution is restricted when it exceeds a threshold
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the flow from evaluation to deployment decision step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Step 1: Measure your abilities
steps.body: As the model improves, we run evaluations to measure its capabilities. Evaluation should also be scalable, as advances in inference capabilities frequently improve models without requiring significant new training. So as we grow our suite of automated assessments, our experts conduct in-depth evaluations to ensure they are measuring the right things.

steps.title: Step 2: Determine whether the threshold has been reached
steps.body: Based on the evaluation results, determine whether the model has reached the High or Critical capability threshold. Automated assessments provide indicators of reaching thresholds, and expert assessments confirm this. The determination that a threshold has been reached is the signal that triggers subsequent steps.

steps.title: Step 3: Design safeguards and review sufficiency
steps.body: Once there, design safeguards that sufficiently reduce the risk, and review whether those safeguards are actually sufficient. The safeguards report details how the safeguards were designed and verified to be effective, and SAG reviews the capability report and safeguards report together to assess residual risk.

steps.title: Step 4: If not enough, withhold or limit
steps.body: If we determine that safeguards are not sufficient, we will conduct further evaluation, request stronger protections, or withhold deployment. From the user's perspective, it may appear that certain features are not available for a certain period of time or are provided on a conditional basis.

steps.title: Step 5: Approve and re-evaluate if sufficient
steps.body: Approve if deemed sufficient, but re-evaluate if new evidence emerges. It is important to note that approval is not permanent. The document also separately addresses cases where other developers release high-risk systems without similar safeguards. In this case, even if the requirements are adjusted, it is stipulated that the risk environment must first be strictly confirmed to have actually changed, the adjustments must be disclosed publicly, and the safeguards must be maintained at a more protective level.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the flow, let's connect it to our usage plan and summarize it in one paragraph.

screens.title: The framework is a commitment to control by level of competency.
screens.lead: Let's tie the content of this lesson into a usage plan perspective. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: The Preparedness Framework is a commitment to track risks limited to frontline capabilities that can cause extreme damage and to set different safeguard requirements depending on capability level. Risk areas are divided into tracking categories of biology and chemistry, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement, and research categories that are still in the preparatory stage.

When reaching High, safety measures are required before deployment, and when reaching Critical, even during development. The sufficiency of safeguards is reviewed by SAG, and management makes the final decision. If there isn't enough, distribution may be withheld or limited.

From a usage planning perspective, there are two conclusions. Because the provider's safety judgment may affect the features and conditions under which we can use them, if we rely on core features, we need to decide in advance what alternatives we will have and how we will respond to changes. And since this framework does not manage day-to-day business risks for us, risks such as customer information and misuse must be addressed separately within our organization's controls.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: A provider's framework is a promise they make to keep, and our organization's controls are a promise we must keep. Place the two together and check for gaps.

checks.intro: Find out what ability threshold means. Just choose the explanation that suits you best. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: In the OpenAI Preparedness Framework, what are the appropriate requirements when a model reaches a high capability level?
options: There is no requirement during development, and safety devices only need to be installed after release.
Since it is at the level of opening a new path, safety measures are needed from the development stage.
The development team makes deployment decisions alone without review by the safety advisory group.
Safety measures must be in place to sufficiently reduce risk before deployment.
checks.correctFeedback: We pinpointed the point of high level demand.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This choice either mixes the needs of High and Critical or misunderstands the structure of the review.
checks.explain: High is a level that can amplify extreme damage through existing routes, and sufficient safety measures are required before deployment. Those who require safety devices even during development are Critical.

wrong.0: High must have safeguards in place before distribution.
wrong.1: Opening unprecedented new paths is the definition of Critical.
wrong.2: A safety advisory group reviews sufficiency and management makes the final decision.

checks.intro: Summarize the flow of distribution decisions. Just place the four items in the correct order.
checks.q: Order the distribution decision flow for models that have exceeded the capability threshold.
items: Measure ability through automated evaluation and expert in-depth evaluation
Determine whether the ability threshold has been reached
If reached, design safety devices and review sufficiency.
Approve if sufficient and re-evaluate if new evidence emerges.
checks.correctFeedback: The flow from measurement to re-evaluation has been arranged correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Rethink the back and forth of measuring capabilities, determining thresholds, reviewing safeguards, and approving.
checks.explain: This is followed by measurement, determination of thresholds, review of safeguards, approval and re-evaluation, and if not sufficient, further evaluation or withholding of deployment.

glossary.def: These are the categories of capabilities that the framework addresses. It is divided into tracking categories of biology/chemistry, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement, and research categories that are still in the preparatory stage.
These are competency levels where safety requirements vary, such as High and Critical. High refers to an amplification of an existing path, and Critical refers to an unprecedented new path.
This is a protective measure to sufficiently reduce the risk of extreme harm. Examples include protection against malicious users, protection against misaligned models, and security controls.
Release approval is given after reviewing the sufficiency of safety devices. SAG reviews and management makes the final decision.

misconceptions.myth: The provider's framework is independent of the average product user.
misconceptions.fact: Thresholds and safeguard conditions affect which features a provider provides, when and under what conditions. If your usage plans depend on certain features, you need to read this promise.

misconceptions.myth: This framework covers all the risks of AI.
misconceptions.fact: Limited scope to frontline abilities that can lead to extreme damage. Persuasion risks should be handled through other means, such as model specifications and usage restrictions, and routine business risks should be managed separately.

misconceptions.myth: Once the threshold is crossed, the model disappears immediately.
misconceptions.fact: If the threshold is exceeded, it becomes a condition to have a safety device. If there are sufficient safeguards, they are deployed; if not, they are withheld or restricted, and reassessed as new evidence emerges.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: A framework is a document that commits to governance by competency level.
Risk areas are divided into tracking and research categories.
High requires safety measures before deployment, and Critical requires safety measures even during development.
Deployments are subject to safeguards sufficiency review, management decisions, and reevaluation as new evidence becomes available.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where do the provider’s safety judgments tie into our usage plans? If you have work that depends on a specific feature, think of alternatives when that feature is limited.
